name: Matthew
author: Matthew (Levi), the tax collector and apostle
introduction:
The Gospel according to Matthew stands at the forefront of the New Testament, serving as a profound link between the Old and New Covenants. It portrays Jesus as the anticipated Messiah and King who fulfills all the prophecies and hopes of Israel, while also establishing a kingdom that surpasses ethnic divisions. Targeted mainly at a Jewish readership, Matthew’s account is richly embedded with Old Testament citations and references, conclusively affirming Jesus as the awaited descendant of Abraham and David who brings the covenant narrative to its definitive fulfillment.

Matthew carefully arranges his narrative, dividing Jesus’ teachings into five significant discourses that correspond to the five books of Moses. This design presents Jesus as a new and greater Moses, who authoritatively explains God’s law and sets forth the righteousness required in the kingdom of heaven. The recurring phrase "that it might be fulfilled" punctuates the Gospel, highlighting Matthew’s key message: Jesus is not a new development but the fulfillment of God’s redemptive plan as revealed in Scripture. From the genealogy establishing Jesus’ royal heritage to the Great Commission extending His authority worldwide, Matthew offers a full depiction of messianic kingship.

However, this is not merely a political declaration. Matthew reveals that the kingdom Jesus proclaims arrives in surprising ways—through humility and service rather than conquest, through suffering instead of immediate triumph, through a cross rather than a throne initially. The religious leaders who should have welcomed their Messiah reject Him, prompting Jesus to redirect the kingdom from ethnic Israel to a new community, the church, founded on the confession of Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God." Empowered by Jesus’ continuing presence, this community receives the mandate to disciple all nations.

The Gospel ends not in defeat over Jewish rejection but in victory: the risen King proclaims, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me," and promises to be with His followers "always, to the very end of the age." Matthew thus lays both a theological foundation for understanding Jesus’ messianic identity and a practical blueprint for the church’s life and mission until His return.

key_themes.theme: Jesus as the Promised Messiah and King
key_themes.description: Matthew provides compelling evidence that Jesus fulfills the Old Testament’s messianic prophecies, from His descent from David to His virgin birth, from His ministry in Galilee to His triumphal entry into Jerusalem. He is the King of the Jews who legitimately claims David’s throne, though His kingdom unfolds in unexpected ways—through suffering and service before ultimate glory.

The frequent use of the phrase "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken" emphasizes that Jesus’ entire life—His birth, ministry, rejection, death, and resurrection—achieves God’s redemptive plan as revealed in Scripture. Matthew demonstrates that the Old Testament finds its true meaning and completion in Christ, who embodies the true Israel.

Central to Jesus’ message is the announcement that "the kingdom of heaven is near." This kingdom represents God’s sovereign rule breaking into history through Jesus’ person and work. The Sermon on the Mount reveals the kingdom’s moral standards; the parables disclose its surprising character; and Jesus’ miracles display its power. Though inaugurated at Jesus’ first coming, the kingdom awaits its full consummation at His return.

Matthew arranges Jesus’ teaching into five discourses paralleling the Pentateuch, depicts Jesus ascending a mountain to deliver the kingdom’s law as Moses did Sinai’s law, and presents Him as the prophet like Moses promised by God. Yet Jesus surpasses Moses—He speaks with divine authority, interpreting the law authoritatively and perfectly embodying the righteousness He commands.

When Israel’s leaders reject Jesus, He declares His intention to build "my church" upon the confession that He is the Christ, the Son of God. This new community, composed of Jews and Gentiles who acknowledge Jesus as King, becomes the people through whom God’s purposes continue in history. The church holds the keys of the kingdom and exercises discipline under Christ’s authority.

key_themes.theme: The Great Commission and Universal Mission
key_themes.description: Matthew’s Gospel transitions from Jesus’ initial focus on "the lost sheep of Israel" to the Great Commission’s command to "make disciples of all nations." The presence of Gentile figures like the magi, the centurion, and the Canaanite woman anticipates this expansion. The risen Christ’s final words empower the church to disciple all peoples, baptizing and teaching them, with the assurance of His ongoing presence.

key_themes.theme: Righteousness Exceeding that of the Scribes and Pharisees
key_themes.description: Jesus demands a righteousness that goes beyond external compliance with the law. The Sermon on the Mount penetrates beneath outward actions to the heart’s motives—the kingdom requires inner transformation of desires, not mere rule-keeping. Genuine righteousness springs from love for God and neighbor, fulfilling the law’s true intent rather than evading it through technicalities.

Matthew stresses that kingdom citizens will be held accountable for their response to Jesus and their treatment of others. Parables about judgment—such as the wheat and tares, the dragnet, the sheep and goats, and the talents—warn that mere profession without obedience is worthless. The King will return to separate the righteous from the wicked, rewarding the faithful and condemning those who reject Him.

key_verses.text: And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
key_verses.significance: This angelic announcement reveals Jesus' mission: He comes not primarily as political liberator but as Savior from sin. The name **Jesus (Yeshua)** means "the LORD saves," identifying His work with God's own saving action. Salvation from sin's guilt and power is the foundation of all gospel blessings.

key_verses.text: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
key_verses.significance: Jesus declares His relationship to the Old Testament: He fulfills the law and prophets by accomplishing what they anticipated, embodying what they required, and authoritatively interpreting their true meaning. The Old Testament is not abolished but completed in Christ, who is its goal and substance.

key_verses.text: And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God... And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
key_verses.significance: Peter's confession represents the foundational truth upon which Christ builds His church: Jesus is the Messiah and the divine Son of God. Jesus promises that His church, built on this confession, will prove indestructible—even the powers of death cannot overcome it. This passage reveals the church's origin, foundation, and assured victory.

key_verses.text: And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.
key_verses.significance: The Great Commission concludes Matthew's Gospel with Jesus' claim to **universal authority** and His commission of the church to disciple all nations. The Trinitarian baptismal formula and the emphasis on teaching obedience provide the church's marching orders. Christ's promise of perpetual presence transforms mission from burden to privilege—we serve empowered by His abiding presence.

outline.section: Birth and Preparation of the King
outline.description: The genealogy traces Jesus’ lineage back to Abraham and David, establishing His rightful place in Israel’s history. The account of the virgin birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, confirming divine intervention. The visit of the magi, Gentiles seeking the newborn King, highlights the kingdom’s broader reach. Jesus’ family flees to Egypt, fulfilling Hosea 11:1, and later returns to settle in Nazareth. John the Baptist prepares the way, and Jesus’ baptism affirms divine approval. His subsequent temptation in the wilderness demonstrates His victory where Israel failed. The narrative concludes with the start of Jesus’ Galilean ministry, proclaiming the nearness of the kingdom.

outline.section: First Discourse: The Sermon on the Mount
outline.description: Jesus unfolds kingdom ethics and the nature of righteousness. The Beatitudes describe the character of kingdom citizens, while the metaphors of salt and light reveal their influence. Jesus clarifies His relationship to the law, emphasizing fulfillment rather than abolition. He calls for a righteousness that goes deeper—addressing anger, lust, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love for enemies. Authentic devotion is shown in giving, prayer, and fasting. The discourse stresses undivided loyalty to God, trust over anxiety, wise judgment, and the necessity of putting Jesus’ words into practice rather than mere hearing.

Ten miracles showcase Jesus’ authority over sickness, nature, demons, and death. He cleanses lepers, heals paralysis, calms storms, casts out demons, forgives sins, and raises the dead. These powerful acts confirm His messianic claims and fulfill Isaiah 35:5-6’s prophetic vision. Jesus’ authority extends to every realm, demonstrating His divine power and validating His message.

Jesus commissions the twelve apostles to minister specifically to Israel, granting them authority to heal and expel demons. He instructs them to travel lightly and rely on hospitality, warning them of impending persecution. Jesus exhorts fearless confession of faith and outlines the cost of discipleship—taking up the cross and risking life to find true life. He promises rewards for those who welcome His messengers.

Jesus faces increasing rejection from Israel’s leaders. John the Baptist’s inquiry and Jesus’ response highlight His identity. Jesus pronounces woes on unrepentant cities and invites the weary to find rest in Him. Controversies arise over Sabbath observance, and Jesus is accused of demonic power, introducing the concept of the unforgivable sin. He challenges demands for miraculous signs and redefines His true family as those who do God’s will.

outline.section: Third Discourse: Parables of the Kingdom
outline.description: Seven parables unveil the mysteries of the kingdom. The sower illustrates varied responses to the word; the wheat and tares depict the coexistence of true and false until judgment; the mustard seed and leaven reveal surprising, hidden growth; the hidden treasure and pearl emphasize the kingdom’s incomparable value; and the dragnet portrays the final separation of the righteous and wicked. Parables conceal truth from hardened hearts while revealing it to receptive followers.

The narrative focuses more closely on the disciples. Jesus miraculously feeds 5,000, demonstrating Messianic provision, and walks on water, revealing His divine nature. He confronts Pharisees over tradition and commends the faith of a Canaanite woman, foreshadowing Gentile inclusion. Another feeding of 4,000 occurs. Peter boldly confesses Jesus as the Christ and Son of God. Jesus predicts His passion for the first time and is transfigured, offering a glimpse of His glory and confirming His identity.

outline.section: Fourth Discourse: Life in the Community
outline.description: Jesus teaches about relationships within the church community. He emphasizes humility and childlike trust, warns against causing others to stumble, and encourages seeking the lost. He outlines the process of church discipline, the authority to bind and loose, the power of agreement in prayer, and teaches forgiveness through the parable of the unforgiving servant, calling believers to forgive as they have been forgiven.

Jesus’ final journey to Jerusalem intensifies conflict with religious leaders. He teaches on marriage and divorce, blesses children, and warns the rich young ruler about the dangers of wealth. The parable of the laborers in the vineyard teaches about grace. Jesus predicts His passion multiple times and addresses requests for honor, teaching that greatness in the kingdom comes through service. He heals blind men and makes a triumphal entry into Jerusalem. He cleanses the temple, faces challenges to His authority, and delivers parables condemning religious leaders. Controversies over taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment arise. Jesus questions the Messiah’s identity and pronounces seven woes on scribes and Pharisees, ending with a lament over Jerusalem.

Jesus delivers prophetic teaching about the end times. He predicts the temple’s destruction and describes signs preceding the end, likening them to birth pains. He warns of great tribulation and the coming of the Son of Man. The parable of the fig tree calls for discernment. Jesus urges watchfulness and readiness through parables of the faithful servant, ten virgins, and talents. The discourse concludes with the judgment of the nations, separating the sheep from the goats based on care for "these my brethren."

The narrative recounts Jesus’ suffering, death, and resurrection. A plot to kill Him unfolds; He is anointed at Bethany; Judas betrays Him. The Last Supper institutes the Lord’s Supper. Jesus predicts Peter’s denial and prays in Gethsemane, submitting to the Father’s will. He is arrested and tried before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin; Peter denies Him; Judas repents and takes his own life. Jesus is tried before Pilate and crucified, crying out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" He dies; the temple veil is torn; a centurion confesses His innocence. Jesus is buried; guards are posted at the tomb. The resurrection is announced by an angel; Jesus appears to women; guards are bribed to spread false reports. The Gospel closes with the Great Commission, as the risen Lord declares all authority and commands making disciples of all nations, promising His continual presence.

historical_context:
The Gospel of Matthew was composed primarily for Jewish Christians and interested Jews, as shown by its numerous Old Testament quotations—about 60 direct citations plus many allusions—its attention to Jewish customs and disputes, and its focus on Jesus as the fulfillment of messianic prophecy. Early church tradition unanimously attributes this Gospel to Matthew (also called Levi), the tax collector called by Jesus to be one of the twelve apostles (9:9; 10:3). Matthew’s background as a tax collector suggests he was literate, skilled in record-keeping, and familiar with both Jewish and Greco-Roman cultures, equipping him well to write this Gospel.

The date of writing is debated, with scholars proposing a range from AD 50 to 70. An earlier date would make Matthew possibly the first Gospel written, though many scholars support Markan priority. A date before AD 70 is inferred from the Gospel’s silence about the temple’s destruction, an event that would have strongly confirmed Jesus’ prophetic warnings had it already occurred. The Gospel addresses a pressing issue for first-century Jewish Christians: how to understand Israel’s rejection of Jesus and the inclusion of Gentiles in God’s people. Matthew answers by demonstrating that this development was neither accidental nor an afterthought but the fulfillment of Scripture and God’s plan.

The Gospel reflects tensions between the emerging church and synagogue Judaism, especially in Jesus’ disputes with Pharisees and His pronouncement of woes against scribes and Pharisees (chapter 23). Yet Matthew insists that Jesus came to fulfill, not abolish, the law and the prophets. The church is not a replacement for Israel but the community of Jews and Gentiles who recognize Jesus as Messiah and inherit the promises made to Abraham. Matthew thus provides theological grounding for the church’s identity as it relates to Judaism and expands to the Gentile world.
literary_style:
Matthew exhibits refined literary artistry and deliberate theological structure. Most notably, the Gospel organizes Jesus’ teaching into five major discourses, each concluding with a formula such as "when Jesus had finished these sayings" (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). These five discourses—the Sermon on the Mount, Mission Instructions, Parables of the Kingdom, Community Life, and the Olivet Discourse—likely correspond intentionally to the five books of Moses (the Pentateuch), portraying Jesus as the new and greater Moses who reveals God’s will with authority.

The Gospel alternates between narrative and discourse sections, with narrative passages providing context and demonstrations of Jesus’ authority, while discourse passages present His authoritative teaching. Geographically, the narrative moves from Galilee (chapters 4-18) to Jerusalem (chapters 19-28), and thematically from Jesus’ initial presentation to Israel (focusing on "the lost sheep of Israel") to the establishment of the church and the mission to all nations. This progression from particular to universal, from Jewish to Gentile inclusion, shapes the entire work.

Matthew frequently employs the phrase "that it might be fulfilled" (or similar expressions) at key moments, explicitly linking Jesus’ life to Old Testament prophecy: His virgin birth (1:22-23), birth in Bethlehem (2:5-6), flight to Egypt (2:15), residence in Nazareth (2:23), Galilean ministry (4:14-16), healing ministry (8:17), gentle demeanor (12:17-21), teaching in parables (13:35), and triumphal entry (21:4-5), among others. This technique affirms that Jesus’ entire life fulfills Scripture, not just isolated events.

The Gospel also uses numerical patterns and symbolic arrangements. The genealogy is divided into three sets of fourteen generations (1:17). There are ten miracles in chapters 8-9, seven parables in chapter 13, and seven woes in chapter 23. Matthew groups teachings thematically, such as the six antitheses in the Sermon on the Mount (“You have heard... but I say”), for memorable presentation. The book begins and ends with the theme of God’s presence: Jesus is "Emmanuel, God with us" at His birth (1:23) and promises "I am with you always" at the conclusion (28:20), forming an inclusio that frames the entire Gospel.
theological_significance:
Matthew offers the most comprehensive New Testament presentation of Jesus as the Jewish Messiah who fulfills Old Testament expectations while surpassing them. The genealogy establishes Jesus’ legal claim to David’s throne through Joseph’s lineage, while the virgin birth explains how Jesus is David’s Son yet greater than David, conceived by the Holy Spirit. Jesus fulfills not isolated prophecies but the entire pattern of Israel’s history: like Israel, He is called out of Egypt; like Moses, He delivers God’s law; like David, He is the anointed King; like the prophets, He speaks God’s word with authority; like the temple, He embodies God’s presence.

The Gospel’s Christology is notably exalted: Jesus is Emmanuel (God with us), the Son of God uniquely related to the Father, the Son of Man who will come in glory to judge the world, and the Lord possessing all authority in heaven and earth. Yet He is also the Servant who came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many (20:28). Matthew presents a Christology that unites full deity and true humanity, sovereignty and servanthood, present humiliation and future exaltation.

Matthew’s ecclesiology is foundational. Only Matthew records Jesus’ explicit promise to build His "church" (16:18; 18:17), portraying it as the community founded on the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The church holds the "keys of the kingdom" (16:19)—the authority to proclaim the gospel that opens the kingdom to believers and binds the unrepentant. The church exercises discipline (18:15-20) under Jesus’ authority and presence. This community transcends ethnic boundaries, incorporating "all nations" through baptism and discipleship (28:19-20).

The Gospel’s eschatology balances present inauguration and future consummation. The kingdom of heaven has drawn near in Jesus’ person and work; it is already breaking into history. Yet it awaits full realization when the Son of Man returns in glory. The parables reveal that the kingdom comes in unexpected ways—beginning small (mustard seed), working quietly (leaven), mixed with opposition (wheat and tares), requiring sacrifice (hidden treasure, pearl). Disciples live in the tension between the ages, enjoying kingdom blessings now while anticipating the King’s return for judgment and reward.

Matthew’s soteriology emphasizes that Jesus came to "save His people from their sins" (1:21). His death is a ransom freeing from sin’s bondage (20:28), and His blood establishes the new covenant for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). Salvation comes through faith in Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God (16:16), producing obedience to His teaching. Matthew stresses that genuine faith results in doing what Jesus commands—profession without practice is worthless (7:21-23). The Gospel’s final scene commissions the church to make disciples who obey all Jesus commanded (28:20).
christ_in_book:
Matthew depicts Jesus wearing multiple messianic titles, fulfilling a variety of Old Testament expectations in one person. He is the Son of David, the rightful King who will reign on David’s throne forever (1:1; 21:9). He is the Son of Abraham, through whom all nations will be blessed (1:1; 8:11). He is Emmanuel, God with us (1:23), the divine presence dwelling among His people. He is the Son of God, uniquely related to the Father, doing His will and revealing His character (3:17; 11:27; 16:16).

Jesus is the new Moses, ascending the mountain to deliver the kingdom’s law (chapters 5-7), yet speaking with inherent authority rather than delegated authority ("But I say unto you"). He is the Suffering Servant of Isaiah, who bears our infirmities and diseases (8:17), who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick (12:20), and who gives His life as a ransom for many (20:28). He is the Son of Man, possessing authority on earth to forgive sins (9:6) and who will come on the clouds of heaven with power and glory to judge the world (24:30; 25:31-46).

Matthew presents Jesus as the perfect Prophet who speaks God’s word with authority, the ultimate Priest who offers His life as a sacrifice for sin and whose blood inaugurates the new covenant (26:28), and the eternal King who holds all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). His kingdom arrives by an unexpected path—through rejection, suffering, and death—before final vindication in resurrection and exaltation. Yet even in humiliation, Jesus exercises divine authority: forgiving sins, calming storms, raising the dead, and claiming equality with the Father.

The Gospel emphasizes that Jesus fulfills Israel’s story. He recapitulates Israel’s history but succeeds where Israel failed: He is the true Son called out of Egypt who remains obedient, the faithful Israel who does not test God in the wilderness, the obedient Son who perfectly keeps the law. Thus, He is not only Israel’s Messiah but the true Israel in whom God’s purposes for His people are accomplished. The kingdom promised to Israel is now mediated through Jesus and extended to all who confess Him as Christ and Lord.
relationship_to_new_testament:
As the first book of the New Testament, Matthew serves as a crucial bridge linking Old Testament promises to their fulfillment in Jesus and laying the groundwork for understanding the church’s relationship to Israel. Its emphasis on Jesus as the Jewish Messiah who fulfills the law and the prophets makes it the ideal introduction to the New Testament canon.

Matthew shares much content with Mark and Luke—the Synoptic Gospels—but with distinct emphases. Mark portrays Jesus primarily as the Suffering Servant, Luke as the Savior of all humanity, while Matthew highlights Jesus as the Davidic King and authoritative Teacher. Matthew incorporates Mark’s action-oriented narrative but adds extensive teaching material, especially the five major discourses. Compared to Luke’s Gentile focus, Matthew maintains stronger Jewish connections while still opening the message to all nations.

Matthew’s Gospel parallels John’s high Christology in affirming Jesus’ divine identity, though with different emphases. Whereas John explicitly declares Jesus’ pre-existence and deity in the Prologue (John 1:1-18), Matthew demonstrates Jesus’ divine Sonship through His miraculous conception, exercise of divine authority, and claim to possess all power in heaven and earth. Both Gospels present Jesus as uniquely revealing the Father.

Matthew’s focus on Jesus’ teaching provides a foundation for apostolic instruction found in the epistles. The Sermon on the Mount shapes New Testament ethics. Jesus’ words about the church (16:18; 18:15-20) inform church order discussed in the Pastoral Epistles. The Great Commission (28:18-20) explains the apostolic mission described in Acts and the letters. Matthew’s emphasis on Jesus as fulfillment of the law connects with Paul’s arguments in Romans and Galatians regarding the law’s role and Christ’s relation to it.

Matthew’s eschatological teaching, especially the Olivet Discourse (chapters 24-25), provides essential background for understanding the eschatology of the epistles and Revelation. The parables of judgment inform New Testament teaching on final accountability. The promise of Jesus’ return in glory to judge and establish His kingdom undergirds Christian hope throughout the New Testament.
practical_application:
Matthew confronts readers with the kingship of Jesus and calls for wholehearted allegiance. Since Jesus holds all authority in heaven and on earth, every aspect of life must submit to His lordship. The Gospel challenges superficial or partial commitment. To confess Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" means yielding to His teaching, obeying His commands, and engaging in His mission. Matthew’s Jesus demands and merits full devotion.

The Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5-7) presents kingdom ethics that penetrate beyond outward behavior to the heart’s attitudes. Jesus calls for righteousness that surpasses mere rule-keeping—a transformation of desires producing purity, mercy, peacemaking, and hunger for righteousness. This teaching confronts shallow religion that manages appearances while harboring anger, lust, greed, and pride. True discipleship requires heart change that only the King can accomplish through His Spirit.

Matthew stresses the necessity of doing what Jesus commands (7:21-27; 28:20), challenging any division between faith and works. Genuine faith produces obedience; profession without practice is worthless. Hearing Jesus’ words without acting on them is like building on sand—the foundation will fail when trials come. Yet the Gospel avoids legalism by rooting obedience in relationship with Jesus and reliance on His grace. We obey because we know, love, and have been forgiven by Him.

The Great Commission (28:18-20) remains the church’s mandate. Making disciples of all nations—teaching them to observe all Jesus commanded and baptizing them in the Triune name—is not optional but the mission of the risen King. This task is possible because "all authority has been given to me" and hopeful because "I am with you always." The same authority and presence that commissioned the first disciples empower the church today.

Matthew’s teaching on prayer, trust, and God’s care (6:5-15, 25-34; 7:7-11) addresses the anxieties and material concerns common in life. Jesus calls believers to seek first God’s kingdom and righteousness, trusting that the heavenly Father knows their needs and will provide. This requires training ourselves to pray for God’s name to be honored, His kingdom to come, and His will to be done—prioritizing His glory above our comfort.

The Gospel’s warnings about judgment and accountability (7:21-23; 13:40-43, 47-50; 25:31-46) remind believers that profession of faith will be tested. How we respond to Jesus’ teaching, how we treat "these my brethren," and how we steward our talents and opportunities all have eternal significance. These warnings are meant to motivate faithful service and genuine transformation, not paralyzing fear. The King will return; we must be prepared.

Matthew emphasizes the importance of church community. Believers are not isolated individuals but members of the body Christ is building. The church provides a context for growth, accountability through discipline, corporate prayer, and mutual care. Matthew 18 portrays a community marked by humility, concern for the weak, restoration of the erring, and mutual forgiveness—"seventy times seven." This vision challenges individualism and nominalism alike.

Finally, Matthew offers hope in Jesus’ abiding presence: "I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Whether facing opposition, uncertainty, or the challenges of mission, believers serve a King who has not abandoned them. His presence transforms circumstances, strengthens witness, and guarantees ultimate victory. Until His return in glory, we live as citizens of His kingdom, demonstrating its reality and proclaiming its King to all nations.
